To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
lymphocytes frozen at different times, and stored for various periods of time, transform in a reproducable manner when placed in vitro in the presence of PHA or as a population in the MLR.
lymphocytes can be frozen and stored at -80°C for at least one month without significant loss of their ability to transform in the MLR and with PHA and with specific antigen.
the freezing and storage of cells at low temperatures destroys neutrophils and the remaining population of lymphocytes transforms in a reproducible fashion when placed in culture.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a method for the storage of lymphocytes.
the effect of freezing and storage on the ability of lymphocytes to transform.
the in vitro transformation and the immunological competence of frozen lymphocytes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the in vitro transformation capacity of frozen-stored lymphoid cells is not destroyed by the freezing process.
lymphocytes may be frozen and stored at temperatures below 0°C for at least one year without loss of viability or transformation capacity.
lymphocytes frozen at low temperatures can transform in a manner similar, but not identical, to fresh cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
frozen lymphocytes can be used for the MLR or for transformation with mitogenic substances.
lymphocytes may be stored frozen for long periods of time without loss of their ability to transform in vitro.

lymphocytes frozen in a medium containing glycerol, dimethylsulfoxide and serum, stored for periods of up to 2 years at -80°C, and thawed and cultured in a manner similar or identical to unfrozen cultures, transform in a manner similar in magnitude to the unfrozen controls.
The main takeaway from our work is that
frozen-stored lymphocyte cultures can be used as a tool to investigate the mechanisms of the in vitro transformation response to mitogens and antigens.
the freezing process destroys neutropils and that the resulting cell populations can be used in a variety of in vitro assays.
lymphocytes frozen at low temperatures can be used in the MLR and in culture with PHAG and specific antigens.
